notes: Read the complete fiscal unit, tax-policy context, all sixteen candidates and the review. Named the U.S. federal government and officials, normalized broken-government, bills-due and bankruptcy metaphors while retaining evaluations, preserved the dramatic-action condition on both debt and interest predictions, anchored Obama-administration debt claims and all figures to 2012, named U.S. spending and GDP, and retained evaluative typing for catastrophic projections and the Affordable Care Act price characterization. Restored the concurrent defense-budget-cut allegation.

claims.claim_text: The U.S. federal government is characterized as excessively large and structurally and financially dysfunctional.
For decades, the U.S. federal government is said to have exceeded its core functions and raised spending to unsustainable levels.
U.S. elected officials are characterized as having promised and spent beyond available resources, creating obligations now due.
Unless dramatic action is taken, interest on U.S. national debt is predicted to consume an increasing share of U.S. wealth.
Europe's risk of national bankruptcy is characterized as a warning to the United States.
During the three and a half years preceding the 2012 platform, the Obama administration is said to have cut defense spending while adding $5.3 trillion to U.S. national debt.
U.S. national debt in the 2012 platform is stated as approximately $16 trillion.
That approximately $16 trillion U.S. debt is characterized as the largest in U.S. history as of 2012.
U.S. federal spending in fiscal 2011 is stated as $3.6 trillion, nearly one quarter of U.S. gross domestic product.
Inflation-adjusted U.S. federal spending in fiscal 2011 is said to exceed three times its World War II peak.
Nearly half of U.S. federal dollars spent in fiscal 2011 are said to have been borrowed.
Medicare, Medicaid and Social Security are said to constitute more than 40 percent of U.S. federal spending.
The platform says contemporary U.S. spending and debt levels were harming U.S. job creation and economic growth.
Future U.S. spending-growth projections are characterized as economically and socially catastrophic.
The future U.S. spending-growth projections are said to exclude Affordable Care Act fiscal effects including over $1 trillion in new taxes, multiple mandates and a price characterized as crushing.
